transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose I'm here because... frankly, because no one else seems to be paying attention to what's actually going on, and I just need someone to look at the facts. For months now—really, it's been going on since at least the late spring, maybe even earlier if I look back at my notes—I’ve been seeing this exact same pattern. 

You see, I supervise an administrative office, I have a degree in this, so I know exactly how scheduling and billing systems are supposed to run. I know what a normal error looks like. But suddenly, my sister’s appointments? They just get moved. Out of nowhere. I'll have it confirmed on the calendar, and then I find out it was rescheduled and absolutely no one told me. And the bills! The bills show up wrong, routed to the wrong place, or the amounts are completely off, which never used to happen. 

And when I call to follow up—which I always do, because I keep meticulous records of all this—these people supposedly just "forget" to call me back. I mean, it's one thing if a receptionist misses a message once, we're all human, but this is constant. It's every single time. And everyone around me, my family, the office staff, they just wave their hands and say, "Oh, it’s just clerical mistakes, people are just so busy these days." 

But I know better. I see what's really happening. It's not mistakes. They are intentionally keeping information from me. It's all completely orchestrated to push me out of the loop and push me out of making decisions regarding my sister. I mean, you don't just have this many "accidents" happen to one person unless there is a clear agenda, you know? It’s just so obvious to me that they want me out of the picture, and I've been documenting all of it because I need someone to see what they're doing.
Do you think anyone is actively working against you or trying to harm you in this situation?

Harm me physically? No, I don't think they're going to, you know, attack me in the street or anything like that. But actively working against me? Oh, absolutely. Without a shadow of a doubt. 

Like I was just saying, this isn't just a one-off thing, it's a deliberate campaign. For months now, I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern play out, week after week, and it's impossible to ignore if you're actually paying attention. I'll have my sister’s appointments perfectly scheduled, written down in ink on my planner, and then suddenly they get moved and I'm the only one who isn't notified. The bills show up completely wrong, routed to some old address or with these bizarre charges that make no sense. And the staff... I leave perfectly clear, professional voicemails, and they supposedly just "forget" to call me back. Over and over again. 

It’s infuriating, really. And what truly gets under my skin is that everyone else—my family, the people at the clinic—they all just brush it off. They look at me like I'm overreacting and say, "Oh, it’s just mistakes, they're short-staffed, the system is just so overwhelmed right now, don't take it personally." 

But I know exactly what they are doing. I've run an office for over two decades, I know the difference between a simple filing error and a coordinated freeze-out. I know they’re keeping information from me on purpose. It’s not incompetence, it’s interference. They are actively trying to push me out of the loop and push me out of making any decisions regarding my sister's care. They want me entirely out of the picture so I can't oversee what they're doing, and frankly, it's exhausting having to fight this hard just to stay informed when it's my own sister. I actually brought my binder with me today, I have all the dates and times highlighted if you want to see exactly how they've been doing it...
Have you considered the possibility that these events could be due to mistakes or oversights rather than a deliberate campaign against you?

Well... yes and no. I mean, of course, I’ve *considered* it. I’m a rational person. Like I said, I supervise an administrative office myself. I’ve been doing it for over twenty years. I know what an oversight looks like. I know what happens when someone hits the wrong key on a keyboard or when a new hire files a chart under the wrong letter. I’ve trained dozens of people, so believe me, I am intimately familiar with human error. 

But you have to look at the sheer volume of it. If it were just one appointment getting moved, or just one bill going to the wrong address, or just one phone call slipping through the cracks... fine. I could accept that. I would have accepted that back in May, or maybe June. But it’s not just one thing. It’s a constant, unrelenting pattern. 

I actually have it all tabbed in my binder—the blue tabs are for the scheduling "errors," the yellow tabs are for the billing "mistakes," and the red tabs, well, those are the unreturned phone calls. And when you look at it all laid out like that, chronologically, the statistical probability of all these things happening to the exact same person, regarding the exact same patient, month after month... it’s just not possible. It defies logic. 

And that’s what frustrates me so much about my family. They just want to take the easy way out and say, "Oh, they’re just busy." But they aren't the ones tracking it. They aren't the ones calling the clinic at 9:00 AM on a Tuesday, waiting on hold for twenty-two minutes, leaving a detailed message with someone named Sarah, and then never hearing back. I am. 

So, yes, I’ve considered that they might be mistakes. But I’ve ruled it out. The evidence just doesn't support it. I know what I’m seeing, and I know they are deliberately keeping information from me. They want to push me out of the decision-making process for my sister, and they’re using this facade of administrative incompetence to do it. It’s the perfect cover, really, because who questions clerical errors these days? But I do. Because I know better.
Do you think there's any possibility that your interpretation of these events might be incorrect?

Incorrect? Honestly, Doctor... no. I really, truly don't. And I know how that sounds, believe me, I do. I know that when someone sits in a chair like this and says they are absolutely certain of something, people tend to raise an eyebrow. My own brother did that just last Sunday at dinner! But you have to understand my position here. 

I am here today, talking to you, precisely because for months now—since at least April, maybe even late March if we look at the very first instance in my binder—I have been seeing this exact same pattern. It is undeniably consistent. I mean, think about it... my sister's appointments get moved without a single notification to me, the primary contact. The bills show up completely wrong, with these baffling routing errors that just happen to delay my access to them. And the staff... they just conveniently "forget" to call me back. Every. Single. Time. 

And even when everyone around me, from my family to the clinic manager, says it’s just mistakes, that I'm just reading too much into normal administrative hiccups... I know they are keeping information from me. I know it in my bones, and I know it from my data. They are trying to push me out of the decisions regarding my sister's care. 

If I were incorrect, the errors would be random, wouldn't they? A missed call here, a wrong address there, affecting different people, different patients. But they aren't random. They are entirely focused on cutting me out. It's a concerted effort. So no, I don't think my interpretation is incorrect. I think I'm the only one actually looking at the reality of the situation, and I just won't let them get away with it.
Do you believe that the people involved in your sister's care are specifically targeting you?

Targeting me? Well, yes, exactly! That is precisely what I have been trying to explain this whole time. I know I probably sound like a broken record, repeating myself over and over, but that is quite literally why I am sitting here in this office talking to you today. 

Because for months now, I have been seeing this exact same pattern play out. It’s my sister’s appointments getting moved without my consent, the bills showing up completely wrong, the staff miraculously "forgetting" to call me back... it is all directed at me. And even when everyone else—my brother, the clinic manager, the receptionists—even when they all sit there and try to pacify me by saying it’s just mistakes or short-staffing, I know the truth. I know they are keeping information from me. 

They are specifically targeting me because I am the one who holds them accountable. I’m the one who reads the fine print, and with my background in office administration, I know how things are supposed to run. They don't like that. They don't like someone looking over their shoulder and catching their "errors." So, instead of just doing their jobs correctly, they have decided to target me to try and push me out of the decisions regarding my sister's care. They think if they make it difficult enough, if they lose enough of my messages or route enough paperwork to the wrong place, I’ll just throw my hands up and walk away. But I won't. I am her primary advocate, and I am not going to let them just push me out of the picture just because I demand a basic level of competence.
Do you think others can see this pattern and intention to keep information from you as clearly as you do?

Well, that's the thing, Doctor. That's the truly maddening part of all this. No, they don't see it. Or, rather, they refuse to see it. It’s like I’m standing in a burning building and everyone else is just complaining about the heat while I’m pointing at the flames! 

I mean, I’ve laid it all out for them. I showed my brother the binder just last week—well, I tried to. I opened it right up on the dining room table, right next to the roast chicken, and I said, "Look at this. Look at the blue tabs, look at the yellow tabs." I walked him through the timeline, starting from that first missed call in March, right up to the billing fiasco last Tuesday. And you know what he did? He sighed. He actually sighed, rubbed his temples, and told me I was overthinking it. He said, "They’re just understaffed, Margaret. Everyone is understaffed right now." 

But how can he say that? How can anyone look at this... this mountain of evidence... and just brush it off as incompetence? I’m here, sitting in this office with you, because for months now I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern. It never stops. My sister’s appointments get moved without a word to me, the bills show up wrong, the staff miraculously "forget" to call me back time and time again... and even when everyone, from my own family to the clinic manager, says it’s just mistakes, I know the truth. 

I know they’re keeping information from me. I know they are trying to push me out of decisions regarding my own sister. And it’s so incredibly isolating when no one else will just look at the facts. They just want to live in this naive little bubble where administrative offices are just full of bumbling, well-meaning people making innocent mistakes. But I supervise an office! I know how these things work, and I know when a system is being weaponized against someone. I just wish, for once, someone else would open their eyes and see what is so glaringly obvious to me.
Do you think it's possible that your feelings of being targeted are related to your own thoughts or emotions, rather than an actual plot against you?

My own thoughts or emotions? Doctor, are you... are you suggesting this is all in my head? Because, I have to tell you, that is frankly insulting. It really is. I'm not sitting here spinning fairy tales because I'm feeling... what? Anxious? Stressed? I'm a fifty-nine-year-old professional woman who has managed offices for decades. I don't just invent plots out of thin air because I'm having a bad day! 

Look, I know why you're asking that. It’s what everyone wants to believe, isn't it? It’s easier to think, "Oh, Margaret is just stressed about her sister’s health, she’s just projecting her anxiety onto the poor, innocent clinic staff." But that completely ignores the reality of what is happening! I’m here because for months now I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern. It’s not a feeling. It’s documented fact. My sister’s appointments get moved without my authorization—and I have the original schedule cards to prove it, right here in the red section of my binder. The bills show up wrong, sent to outdated addresses or with inexplicable billing codes that delay everything. And the people at that clinic... they just "forget" to call me back. Time after time after time. 

And even when everyone—my brother, the clinic manager, you, apparently—even when everyone says it’s just mistakes or my own emotions running high... I know they’re keeping information from me. I know it. They are actively trying to push me out of decisions regarding my sister's care because I am the only one holding them to any sort of standard. So no, Doctor, it is not my "emotions." It is a coordinated, deliberate effort to sideline me, and I have the paperwork to prove it, if anyone would just bother to look at it instead of trying to psychoanalyze me!
Have you experienced any major life changes or stressful events recently, aside from the issues with your sister's care?

Major life changes? Stressful events? Well, I suppose that depends entirely on what you consider "major," doesn't it? I mean, life is a series of events, some more taxing than others. But if you're asking if I've, I don't know, gotten divorced, or lost my job, or bought a new house, or started skydiving... no. Nothing like that. 

I’ve been at the same company for fifteen years, supervising the same administrative department, dealing with the same vendors, the same end-of-month reporting cycles... it’s all very structured. Very predictable. Which is exactly why I thrive there. I like order, Doctor. I like things to make sense and follow a logical progression. I like to know that if I file a form in triplicate, it goes to the right three departments. So, my work life is completely stable. My home life is stable. I still live in the same house I’ve owned for twenty years. I still have my book club on the second Thursday of every month, though honestly, lately, I haven't had the energy for Barbara's endless chatter about her grandchildren. 

But aside from that, no. There haven't been any massive upheavals. No sudden traumas or dramatic shifts in my personal life. The only thing... the only thing that is completely chaotic, completely upside down, and causing me any real stress, is this situation with my sister's care. That is the only anomaly in my otherwise very organized, very manageable life. It's just that one glaring issue where everything I know about how systems should work is being completely upended by these people who are, quite frankly, making a mockery of professional standards. So no, nothing else is going on. Just this... this absolute circus they've created around my sister.
Do you feel like you have a special role or mission in uncovering the truth about your sister's care?

A special role? A mission? Well, I wouldn't use words like "mission," Doctor. That makes it sound like I'm some sort of crusader in a cape, or... or someone who watches too many spy movies. I'm just a sister. I'm just a sister who happens to have the administrative background to actually understand what is happening here. 

But... do I feel like I'm the only one who can do this? Yes. Absolutely yes. Because who else is going to do it? My brother? I already told you about him. He just sighs and rubs his temples and makes excuses for them. He doesn't want to rock the boat. He’s always been like that, even when we were kids. If something was difficult, he’d just look the other way. And my sister... well, she’s the patient. She’s vulnerable. She’s not in a position to be auditing billing codes and cross-referencing appointment logs. She just goes where they tell her to go and pays what they tell her to pay. 

So it falls to me. It has to. Because if I don't hold these people accountable, they are just going to keep doing it. They’ll keep moving the appointments, they’ll keep sending the wrong bills, they’ll keep having these little closed-door meetings where they decide what to do with my sister without even consulting me. And I simply cannot allow that. I have thirty years of experience managing offices. I know how a filing system is supposed to work. I know what a standard operating procedure looks like. I know the difference between a clerical error and a deliberate omission. 

So, it's not a "mission," Doctor. It's a responsibility. It's a duty. I am the only one standing between my sister and this... this orchestrated incompetence. I’m the only one who has taken the time to compile the binder, to color-code the tabs, to document every single phone call, every single email, every single time they said they would get back to me and didn't. I have it all right here. And I have to keep doing it, because the moment I stop looking, the moment I let my guard down, they’ll push me out completely. And I just won't let that happen. I can't.
Have you recently started to see patterns or conspiracies in things that you didn't notice before?

Conspiracies? Please, Doctor, let’s not use words like that. It makes it sound like I’m looking for aliens in the backyard or wearing a tin foil hat. I am a rational, educated woman. I am talking about administrative patterns. And yes, as I was just trying to explain to you a moment ago, I have absolutely been seeing a pattern, but it's not something I just "started to see" out of nowhere—it’s been going on for months now. Months! 

I’m here because it is simply impossible to ignore anymore. I am looking at the exact same sequence of events over and over, week after week. Like I said, my sister’s appointments get moved without any notification to me—and I mean, they will call her on a Tuesday morning to change a Thursday afternoon appointment, knowing full well I am in weekly departmental meetings on Tuesdays and can't intercept the call. Then the bills show up wrong. Not just a little wrong, but completely miscoded, which anyone who has ever worked in a front office knows triggers an automatic delay in processing. And then, of course, the staff just magically "forget" to call me back when I try to correct it. I leave voicemails with the front desk, I leave messages with the nursing station, I send emails... nothing. Complete silence. 

And you know, my brother, the clinic manager, even you just a few minutes ago... everyone keeps telling me, "Oh, Margaret, it’s just human error, they’re just mistakes, the healthcare system is overwhelmed right now." Mistakes! A mistake is filing a paper in the wrong folder once. When it happens consecutively for half a year, it is not a mistake. It is a strategy. Even when everyone says it’s just mistakes, I know the truth. I know they are deliberately keeping information from me. They are doing everything in their power to push me out of the decisions regarding my sister's care because they know I am the only one actually watching them. 

So no, I am not seeing "conspiracies" in random things. I am seeing a very specific, very real pattern of behavior directed at me, and quite frankly, if you would just look at the green section of my binder—the section where I've cross-referenced the phone logs with the billing dates—you would see exactly what I mean. It's all right there in black and white.
Do you think you might be misinterpreting things because of your own stress or anxiety?

Stress? Anxiety? Doctor, with all due respect, I supervise an entire administrative department. I handle end-of-month reconciliation, vendor disputes, and personnel scheduling for a very busy office. I know what stress is, and I know how to manage it perfectly well. I don't just start imagining things or misinterpreting reality because I have a lot on my plate. I am a professional. 

So no, I am absolutely not misinterpreting anything. As I was just trying to explain to you, I’m here—sitting in this chair, taking time out of my very busy schedule—because for months now I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern. This isn't a feeling. It is a documented sequence of events. My sister’s appointments get moved without my consent, the bills show up completely wrong, and these people conveniently "forget" to call me back every single time I try to get to the bottom of it. 

And it is frankly insulting that every time I point this out, everyone just pats me on the head and tries to placate me. My brother says it, the clinic manager says it, and now you’re implying it with this question about my anxiety. But I am not a fool, Doctor. Even when everyone says it’s just mistakes, or just administrative hiccups, or just my own stress... I know the truth. I know they are deliberately keeping information from me. They are actively trying to push me out of the decisions regarding my sister's care. They want me gone so they can do whatever they please without anyone holding them to a proper standard. You simply cannot chalk that up to my anxiety when the proof is sitting right here in my binder. It is happening, and I am the only one willing to call it what it is.
Have you ever felt like someone or something was out to get you before this situation with your sister's care?

Before this? No. No, absolutely not. I mean, what a question. You make it sound like I walk around looking over my shoulder, expecting the mailman to steal my identity or the neighbors to be spying on me. I don't live like that. I am a busy, practical woman. I have an entire department to run. So, no, I have never felt like anyone or anything was "out to get me" before all of this started. I've always had excellent working relationships with my colleagues, my vendors, everyone. 

This entire situation—this... this coordinated effort to freeze me out of my sister's medical decisions—it has a very specific timeline. It has been going on for about 11 months. Exactly 11 months, actually. 

It started right around the time my sister’s health suddenly got worse. We had a scare, a very serious scare, and it became immediately clear to me that she could no longer manage her own appointments. She was just too weak, too overwhelmed by the sheer volume of paperwork and referrals. She didn't know what she was signing. So, naturally, as her sister and as someone with my professional background, I had to step in and start coordinating her care. 

I took over the scheduling, the insurance verifications, the specialist referrals... all of it. I treated it like any other project I manage at work. I set up the binder, I established a clear communication protocol with the clinic, I made sure I was listed as her primary contact... and that is exactly when the pushback started. 

Before 11 months ago, I was just her sister. We’d have lunch on Sundays, maybe go to a garden show... I wasn't interacting with her medical team at all. But the moment—the very moment—I stepped in 11 months ago and started asking for accountability, asking to see the actual itemized bills, asking why an appointment was moved without my authorization... that's when they realized I wasn't going to just blindly accept whatever they told me. 

So no, Doctor, this isn't some lifelong complex I have. I am not a paranoid person. This is a very real, very documented situation that began 11 months ago when her health declined and I became the coordinator of her care. Why on earth would I have felt this way before? There was nothing to audit before.
Have you ever felt like you were being unfairly treated or targeted in your work or personal life before this situation with your sister's care?

Unfairly treated at work? Heavens, no. Let me be very clear about how I run my office, Doctor. I have been an administrative supervisor for a long time, and you simply do not get to my level—or maintain a department that handles the kind of volume we do—if you walk around taking every little thing personally or thinking people are out to get you. 

If a vendor disputes an invoice, or if one of my support staff has a grievance about the schedule, I don't feel targeted. I look at the facts. I pull the timecards, I check the purchase orders, and I resolve the issue logically. I have an absolutely stellar track record at my job. Just last quarter, the regional director specifically commended my department's reconciliation process. My colleagues respect me, my staff respects me, and I have excellent relationships in my personal life as well. I really don't have time for drama. Between my career, maintaining my home, and... well, before all this started, my friends and my usual routine, I have a very fulfilling, very stable life. 

So no, I have never felt unfairly treated before. And frankly, that is exactly why this whole situation with my sister’s medical team is so glaringly obvious to me! If I were the sort of person who always felt slighted, or if I didn't know how professional organizations are supposed to run, maybe I wouldn't notice what they are doing. But because I am accustomed to transparent, competent interactions, this... this absolute stonewalling from her clinic stands out like a sore thumb. 

I know what normal workplace friction looks like. I know what a standard clerical error looks like. What they are doing is not that. Because I don't have a history of just making things up or feeling persecuted, you have to understand that when I tell you they are deliberately targeting me now, it is because it is actually happening. I have never had to build a binder like this for anyone else in my entire life, Doctor, because I have never dealt with a group of people so maliciously intent on undermining me.
Have you ever had thoughts like this before, where you felt like someone or something was intentionally working against you?

Doctor, I... are we going in circles? Because I feel like you are asking me the exact same question you just asked, just using slightly different words. 

No. Never. I have never had thoughts like this before. 

If you are trying to find some sort of lifelong pattern where I just imagine people are out to get me, you are going to be very disappointed. I don't go through life thinking the cashier at the grocery store is intentionally shortchanging me, or that the woman at the bank is deliberately holding up my deposits. I just don't have the time or the energy for that kind of thinking. I am a very practical person. When things go wrong—and they do, because life is messy and people make mistakes—I look for the logical explanation. If a vendor at work sends the wrong supplies, I don't think they're "working against me." I think someone in their shipping department misread a SKU number. I pick up the phone, I clarify the error, and we fix it. That is how my brain works. I assume competence until proven otherwise.

It takes an overwhelming amount of evidence for me to finally conclude that someone is intentionally sabotaging me. An absolute mountain of evidence. Which is exactly why you have to understand how serious this situation is with my sister's care team. I didn't just wake up one morning and decide they were working against me because of one lost message. It took months of them ignoring my calls, months of them changing her appointment times without notifying me, months of them refusing to provide the itemized statements I am legally entitled to see as her care coordinator. 

So, no. To answer your question again, I have never had these thoughts before. Because before these past eleven months, I had never encountered a group of people so maliciously determined to block me from doing what needs to be done. I am only having these thoughts now because it is the only logical conclusion to the facts I have gathered in that binder.
Have you been having trouble sleeping or experiencing unusual fatigue lately?

Trouble sleeping? No, no. I mean, you would think I might be tossing and turning, given the sheer level of incompetence and obstruction I am dealing with every single day, but I actually have a very strict evening routine. As an administrative supervisor, you learn very early on in your career that if you do not manage your rest, the workload will just eat you alive. 

So I am extremely disciplined about it. By 9:30 PM, the binder is closed. I put it in my home office, I shut the door, and I absolutely do not look at it again until the next day. I make myself a cup of chamomile tea, I might watch a little bit of the evening news—just the local broadcast, mind you, because the 24-hour cable channels are just designed to agitate people—and I am in bed by 10:15. So my sleep is quite sound. Seven and a half to eight hours, like clockwork. 

And as for fatigue... well, I wouldn't call it unusual fatigue. Am I tired at the end of the day? Of course I am. I run an entire department, I maintain my own home, and I am single-handedly doing the job of three patient care coordinators because my sister's clinic refuses to do theirs. But it is a normal, earned tiredness. It is certainly not some mysterious, unexplained fatigue. I wake up every morning perfectly energized and ready to tackle whatever new roadblock they have tried to throw in my way. I have to be sharp, you see. If I were exhausted or sleep-deprived, I might miss a discrepancy in the billing codes or a subtle change in her chart, and I simply cannot afford to let them slip anything past me.
Have you ever had a period in your life where you believed someone or something was working against you, before this situation with your sister's care?

Doctor, I... honestly, I am starting to feel like I am being cross-examined here. Is there a reason you keep asking me variations of the exact same question? Because I feel like I have been incredibly clear, and yet here we are again, circling back to this idea that I just walk around thinking people are out to get me. 

To be absolutely, perfectly clear—and I really hope this is the last time I have to say this—no. I have never, in my fifty-nine years on this earth, had a period in my life where I believed someone was working against me before this situation with my sister's care. Never. Not once. Not in high school, not in college when I was getting my degree, not in my thirty-plus years in administrative management. 

I don't know what it says in your notes or what you are trying to find, but you are barking up the wrong tree. I am a very grounded, very logical person. I deal in spreadsheets, Doctor. I deal in timecards and invoices and objective reality. If I had a history of paranoia or whatever it is you are trying to imply, do you really think I could have maintained my position as a department supervisor for this long? Do you think I could manage the volume of work I do if I was constantly looking over my shoulder? 

I am only telling you that my sister's clinic is working against me because they *are* working against me. It is not a belief, it is a fact. A fact supported by months of documented evidence, which I have right here in this binder. I really need you to hear what I am saying, instead of trying to fit me into whatever little diagnostic box you have in mind. I have never felt this way before because I have never been treated this way before. It is as simple as that.
Do you feel like you have special powers or insights that help you understand the situation with your sister's care?

Special powers? Oh, Doctor, really. That is... that's almost insulting. No, I don't have "special powers." I'm not a psychic, I'm not reading tea leaves, and I certainly don't have some sort of supernatural insight into what the clinic staff is doing. I mean, honestly, what a question. 

What I have—and this is very different from "special powers," I assure you—is thirty-five years of experience in administrative management. I know how an office is supposed to run. I know how scheduling software works, I know how billing codes are generated, and I know exactly how long it takes for a referral to be processed if the person handling it is actually doing their job. 

So when I call the clinic and the receptionist tells me that the system "glitched" and lost my sister's physical therapy authorization... well, I don't need a crystal ball to know that's a lie. I know that electronic health record systems have audit trails. I know that an authorization doesn't just vanish into thin air without a user logging in and actively deleting or misfiling it. That's not a special power, Doctor. That is basic, fundamental competence in my field. 

And when I see that her appointments keep getting moved to times when they know I have my departmental staff meetings—which I made very clear to them on the initial intake forms, by the way—I don't need a sixth sense to see the pattern. I just need to look at the calendar, which I have cross-referenced with my own work schedule in section four of my binder. I've highlighted every single instance where they've scheduled her right in the middle of my quarterly reviews. It's statistically impossible for it to be a coincidence at this point. 

So, no. No special powers. Just attention to detail. Just the ability to read a spreadsheet, track a timeline, and hold people accountable when they are clearly, deliberately failing to do their jobs. I think it's very telling that when a woman is organized, thorough, and refuses to be lied to, it's suddenly framed as having "special insights" or being paranoid, rather than just being good at what she does. I am just applying the exact same skills I use to run my department to managing my sister's care. That's all it is. Objective, documented facts.
Is there anything that could happen or anything someone could tell you that would make you question your belief that the clinic is intentionally working against you?

Question my belief? Doctor, you have to understand... it’s not just a belief that can be waved away by someone giving me a flimsy excuse. I mean, what could they possibly say at this point?
